title: L versus BPL
formal:
Is \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm L?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
definitions:
A language \(S\) is a set of finite binary strings; put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). A machine has a finite program, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input head cannot move outside the endmarkers. Work tapes are semi-infinite; their heads move by at most one cell per step. Space is the sum of the numbers of distinct work-tape cells visited, including blank cells. The read-only input and finite control are excluded from this count; all stored counters, arithmetic operands, history and auxiliary data are included. Acceptance or rejection is a halting control state, not an additional readable output tape.

A randomized transition can obtain at most one fresh independent fair bit. Past bits cannot be revisited unless retained in counted work space. There is no random-tape address, free clock, oracle, advice, or additional uncounted storage. A deterministic machine has the same tape model and no coin transitions. One ordinary machine transition costs one time step.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{BPL}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and positive integers \(K,C,d\) such that for every input \(x\) and every realization of its random choices, \(R\) visits at most
\[K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
work cells and halts with a bit in at most \(T(n)=C(n+2)^d\) steps. In addition, for every \(x\),
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf 1_S(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
The probability is only over internal coins. Exactly, supply a uniform string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}\), consuming one bit whenever requested and ignoring the unused suffix; the success requirement is
\[3\bigl|\{u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}:R(x;u)=\mathbf1_S(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{T(n)}.\]
This finite counting formula defines the probability; it is not an extra operation available to the machine. The space and time bounds hold on every random string, not merely in expectation. Success is required separately on every member and nonmember, not only for a typical input distribution. No promise excludes inputs with intermediate acceptance probability: a valid decider for \(S\) must meet the appropriate bound on every binary string.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm L\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(D\) and a positive integer \(K'\) such that for every \(x\), \(D\) halts with \(\mathbf1_S(x)\) and visits at most \(K'\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. In this bounded-input-head model there are only polynomially many configurations at a fixed input length. A halting deterministic run cannot repeat a configuration, so a separate polynomial time guarantee follows. The program and its constants may depend on \(S\), but not on the particular input or its length.

The deterministic machine may have a different space constant, time exponent and computation from the randomized decider. Uniformity means a single finite program serves all input lengths, without length-dependent advice. Deterministic machines are a special case of randomized machines, so \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{BPL}\). The question asks for the reverse inclusion of languages; it does not prescribe a pseudorandom-generator construction or a compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions.

context_blocks.text: Logarithmic memory is enough for a constant number of input-position counters but not for storing an arbitrary long random history. Fresh coins can guide the computation without remaining available afterward. Allowing the machine to freely revisit an entire random string changes the resource model, which is why the random-access convention is part of the question.

Saks and Zhou obtained deterministic simulation in \(O((\log n)^{3/2})\) space. Hoza’s Theorem 1.6 improves this to
\[O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\). This remains larger than \(O(\log n)\). These are space bounds; they do not assert that the improved-space simulation also runs in polynomial time.

A read-once branching program is a finite layered computation: each newly read random symbol selects a transition to the next layer, and a designated final state determines the answer. Its width is the number of states per layer and its length is the number of symbols read. This represents the random part of a bounded-space computation after the ordinary input is fixed. Restricted transition structures or unusually short programs need not capture every BPL computation.

An ordinary pseudorandom generator approximates acceptance probabilities using a genuine distribution generated from a short uniform seed. A weighted generator instead associates possibly negative real weights with seeds and approximates acceptance through a signed weighted average. Such estimates can be useful for derandomization, but they are not themselves sampling probabilities. Improving weighted generators does not automatically supply an ordinary generator with identical parameters.

Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction into weighted generators, including dependence on the alphabet size. The revision explicitly attributes the relevant earlier arity/error implication to Cheng and Hoza. It retains the general BPL versus L question as open; neither its weighted output nor the conditional implication supplies the equality here.

Cheng and Wu’s July 2026 version gives \(O(\log w)\)-space derandomization for regular branching programs of width \(w\), length at most \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log w})}\), binary alphabet, and inverse-polynomial additive error. Regularity means that every consecutive-layer transition graph has the same incoming and outgoing degree at every vertex. Both regularity and the short-length regime are genuine hypotheses. The result does not cover arbitrary polynomial-length, polynomial-width programs representing general BPL computations.

why: This asks whether randomness adds computational power when an algorithm can remember only logarithmically many bits of an arbitrarily long input. An equality would permit deterministic bounded-memory decision whenever bounded-error randomized decision is possible; a separation would show an inherent memory advantage of randomness.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the inclusion in the statement, or of its logical negation
\[\exists S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \land\ S\notin\mathrm L.\]
A positive proof must establish a uniform deterministic decider with one logarithmic work-space bound for every language satisfying the full randomized definition. A negative proof must establish one fixed total language with a valid bounded-error randomized decider and exclude every deterministic decider with every constant logarithmic space bound for that language.

Extra polylogarithmic space, a rereadable uncounted random tape, advice, an oracle, a promise-problem separation, or correctness only at selected lengths does not meet this target. A failed generator construction or a lower bound for a restricted family of simulations does not rule out all deterministic deciders. Unproved hardness assumptions yield conditional results only. This is a yes/no class-comparison question with an exact probability threshold, not a numerical approximation target.

importance.reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. The class equality merits a full card even alongside a more specific generator-construction target.

sentences: L contains languages decided by one deterministic machine using logarithmic work space, while BPL permits fresh fair random bits and bounded error.
Random bits are read once unless stored in counted memory, and the randomized machine obeys uniform logarithmic-space and polynomial-time bounds on every run.
The question asks whether every BPL language has a deterministic logarithmic-space decider that is correct on every input.
The best general simulation reviewed here uses more than logarithmic space, and recent weighted-generator and regular-program results retain distinct guarantees or restrictions.
A solution requires a complete Lean proof of the inclusion or a single total language separating the two classes under the stated uniform model.
